interactions.label: A 46,XY individual with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome has functional

params.question: A 46,XY individual with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome has functional testes that produce testosterone, yet the external phenotype is female. Which mechanism best explains this presentation?

answers.text: The SRY gene is non-functional, so the indifferent gonad defaults to an ovary

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The SRY gene is intact in AIS — that is why testes form. The problem lies downstream, at the level of androgen receptors in target tissues.

answers.text: Anti-Müllerian hormone is absent, allowing the Müllerian ducts to persist and develop

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. AMH is produced normally by Sertoli cells, which is why Müllerian structures (uterus, fallopian tubes) are absent in AIS. The female external phenotype results from inability to respond to testosterone.

answers.text: Target tissues lack functional androgen receptors and cannot respond to testosterone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In complete AIS, androgen receptors are non-functional. Although the testes produce normal or elevated testosterone, target tissues cannot respond, so male external genitalia do not develop despite the 46,XY karyotype.

answers.text: Excess aromatase converts all testosterone to oestrogen, driving female external development

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While some testosterone is aromatised to oestradiol physiologically, the primary mechanism in AIS is the absence of functional androgen receptors, not excessive aromatisation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the section on androgen insensitivity syndrome. The key concept is that having testes and producing testosterone is not sufficient for male differentiation — target tissues must also respond through functional androgen receptors.
Excellent! AIS demonstrates that sex differentiation depends not only on hormone production but also on tissue responsiveness — the androgen receptor is the critical link.

interactions.label: A 28-year-old man presents with a left-sided scrotal swelling described as a 'ba

params.question: A 28-year-old man presents with a left-sided scrotal swelling described as a 'bag of worms' and is diagnosed with a varicocele. How does this condition primarily impair his fertility?

answers.text: Dilated veins obstruct the vas deferens, blocking sperm transport to the ejaculatory duct

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A varicocele involves dilation of the pampiniform venous plexus, not obstruction of the vas deferens. The impairment is thermal, not obstructive.

answers.text: Dilated testicular veins disrupt the countercurrent heat exchange, raising scrotal temperature and impairing spermatogenesis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The dilated veins of a varicocele can no longer cool arterial blood via the pampiniform plexus. This raises testicular temperature above the 2–4 °C below core temperature needed for normal spermatogenesis.

answers.text: Venous congestion compresses the epididymis, preventing sperm from gaining motility

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A varicocele does not compress the epididymis. The primary mechanism is disrupted thermoregulation — the dilated veins impair countercurrent heat exchange, raising testicular temperature.

answers.text: Reduced arterial inflow causes ischaemia of the seminiferous tubules and Leydig cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A varicocele is a venous dilation, not an arterial insufficiency problem. The impaired countercurrent heat exchange raises testicular temperature, which disrupts spermatogenesis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Revisit how the pampiniform plexus functions as a countercurrent heat exchanger. Spermatogenesis requires a temperature 2–4 °C below core body temperature; a varicocele disrupts this cooling and impairs sperm production.

Well done! The pampiniform plexus normally cools arterial blood before it enters the testis. A varicocele undermines this mechanism, illustrating why scrotal thermoregulation is critical for sperm production.

params.question: A bodybuilder who has used exogenous anabolic steroids for two years presents with infertility and bilateral testicular atrophy. Which sequence of events explains his findings?

answers.text: Exogenous testosterone directly damages Sertoli cells, halting their support of spermatogenesis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Exogenous steroids do not directly damage Sertoli cells. The mechanism is indirect — through suppression of LH, which leads to Leydig cell atrophy and loss of the high local testosterone Sertoli cells need.

answers.text: Exogenous testosterone is aromatised to excess oestradiol, which is directly toxic to spermatogonia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While some testosterone is aromatised to oestradiol, direct germ cell toxicity is not the primary mechanism. The central problem is suppression of the HPG axis via negative feedback.

answers.text: Exogenous testosterone suppresses GnRH and LH via negative feedback, causing Leydig cell atrophy and failed spermatogenesis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Exogenous testosterone provides sustained negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, suppressing GnRH and LH. Without LH, Leydig cells atrophy, intratesticular testosterone plummets, and spermatogenesis — which requires high local testosterone — fails.

answers.text: Exogenous testosterone saturates intratesticular androgen receptors, rendering the seminiferous tubules unresponsive

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The problem is not receptor saturation within the testes. Exogenous testosterone reduces GnRH and LH output centrally, depriving Leydig cells of their trophic stimulus and causing atrophy.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the HPG axis feedback loop. Exogenous testosterone suppresses GnRH and LH at the hypothalamic–pituitary level. Without LH stimulation, Leydig cells atrophy, local testosterone drops, and spermatogenesis ceases.

Excellent! This is a classic demonstration of HPG axis negative feedback. The same mechanism explains why steroid users may develop hypogonadism on withdrawal and why fertility often recovers only months after cessation.

interactions.label: The mid-cycle LH surge that triggers ovulation is caused by negative feedback fr

params.question: The mid-cycle LH surge that triggers ovulation is caused by negative feedback from the rising oestrogen produced by the dominant Graafian follicle.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. Although oestrogen usually exerts negative feedback on the HPG axis, the sustained high levels from the dominant Graafian follicle switch to positive feedback. This positive feedback drives the LH surge that triggers ovulation — a critical exception to the usual pattern.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — it is positive feedback, not negative. During most of the cycle, oestrogen exerts negative feedback on GnRH and LH. However, the sustained high oestrogen from the mature Graafian follicle switches to positive feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, triggering the LH surge that ruptures the follicle.

interactions.label: Without human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG), an early pregnancy would fail. Whic

params.question: Without human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG), an early pregnancy would fail. Which function of hCG is essential for maintaining the pregnancy during the first trimester?

answers.text: It stimulates the anterior pituitary to increase progesterone secretion directly

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The anterior pituitary does not produce progesterone. hCG acts on the corpus luteum in the ovary — not the pituitary — to maintain progesterone production.

answers.text: It binds the LH receptor on the corpus luteum, sustaining progesterone production beyond day 26

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. hCG structurally resembles LH and binds the same receptor on luteal cells. This prevents the corpus luteum from degenerating at day 26, maintaining progesterone output until the placenta takes over at around 8–10 weeks.

answers.text: It promotes trophoblast invasion by thinning the endometrial lining for deeper implantation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. hCG does not thin the endometrium. Its critical role is maintaining the corpus luteum so that progesterone keeps the endometrium in its secretory state, supporting the implanted embryo.

answers.text: It suppresses maternal uterine contractions by acting directly on the myometrium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Suppression of uterine contractions in early pregnancy is primarily a function of progesterone, not hCG. The essential role of hCG is to maintain the corpus luteum's progesterone output by binding LH receptors.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the early pregnancy timeline. The trophoblast secretes hCG, which binds LH receptors on the corpus luteum and sustains progesterone production past day 26 — preventing the endometrial shedding that would otherwise terminate the pregnancy.
Well done! The rescue of the corpus luteum by hCG is a pivotal concept in early pregnancy. It also explains why hCG detection in blood and urine is the basis of pregnancy tests.

interactions.label: A patient with vaginal bleeding, a markedly enlarged uterus, and clinical featur

params.question: A patient with vaginal bleeding, a markedly enlarged uterus, and clinical features of a hydatidiform mole has a negative home urine pregnancy test. Quantitative blood testing reveals extremely high β-hCG. What explains the false negative urine result?

answers.text: Molar tissue produces a structurally altered hCG variant that home test antibodies cannot recognise

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Molar tissue produces standard hCG detectable by commercial tests. The false negative is due to the hook effect — antibody saturation at extremely high concentrations — not structural variation.

answers.text: Extremely high hCG concentrations saturate both capture and detection antibodies, preventing sandwich formation (hook effect)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The hook effect occurs when extremely high hCG saturates both antibodies in the immunoassay independently, preventing proper antibody–hCG–antibody complex formation. This is a recognised pitfall in gestational trophoblastic disease.

answers.text: Vaginal bleeding diluted the urine sample below the 20–25 mIU/mL detection threshold

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Vaginal bleeding does not significantly dilute urinary hCG. In molar pregnancy, hCG levels are disproportionately elevated — the false negative results from the hook effect, not from dilution.

answers.text: Home tests detect only intact hCG dimers, and molar tissue secretes predominantly free β-subunits

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Molar tissue produces intact hCG abundantly. The false negative results from the hook effect — a technical limitation of sandwich immunoassays at extremely high analyte concentrations.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the hook effect. At very high hCG concentrations (as in molar pregnancy), excess antigen saturates both antibodies independently in the sandwich assay, preventing complex formation and yielding a false negative result.

Excellent! The hook effect is an important clinical pitfall. Whenever clinical features suggest gestational trophoblastic disease but a home test is negative, a quantitative blood β-hCG should always be requested.

interactions.label: A woman with bilateral fallopian tube blockage from previous pelvic inflammatory

params.question: A woman with bilateral fallopian tube blockage from previous pelvic inflammatory disease undergoes in vitro fertilisation. How does IVF overcome her tubal obstruction?

answers.text: Gonadotrophin injections reduce peritubal adhesions, restoring tubal patency before fertilisation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Gonadotrophin (FSH) injections stimulate ovarian follicle development; they have no effect on tubal adhesions. IVF bypasses the tubes rather than attempting to reopen them.

answers.text: Mature oocytes are retrieved directly from the ovaries by transvaginal aspiration, fertilised in the laboratory, and embryos are transferred to the uterine cavity — bypassing the tubes entirely

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In IVF, FSH injections stimulate multiple follicles, and mature oocytes are retrieved directly from the ovaries. Fertilisation occurs in the laboratory, and embryos are transferred into the uterine cavity — the fallopian tubes are bypassed completely.

answers.text: Intracytoplasmic sperm injection places sperm directly into the uterine cavity, avoiding tubal transport

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. ICSI involves injecting a single sperm directly into an oocyte in the laboratory — not into the uterus. It is used for severe male factor infertility, not to bypass tubal obstruction.

answers.text: Embryo transfer stimulates neovascularisation around the occluded tubes, gradually restoring their function

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Embryo transfer does not restore tubal function. IVF works precisely because it bypasses the fallopian tubes altogether — oocytes are retrieved from the ovaries and embryos are placed directly in the uterus.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the IVF procedure. The key insight is that IVF bypasses the fallopian tubes entirely: oocytes are retrieved from the ovaries, fertilised outside the body, and embryos are transferred directly into the uterine cavity.

Well done! Understanding IVF's mechanism — ovarian stimulation, oocyte retrieval, in vitro fertilisation, and direct embryo transfer — explains how it circumvents tubal obstruction, the most common structural cause of female infertility.
